questions.question: A payslip shows a gross salary of R10 500,00, with deductions of PAYE R840,00, UIF R105,00 and pension R525,00. Calculate the net income, add the household's other income of R1 100,00 rent and R1 070,00 from Saturday hair work, and explain why the gross figure may never be used in a budget.
questions.expected_answer: Total deductions: R840 + R105 + R525 = R1 470,00. Net income: R10 500 − R1 470 = R9 030,00. Total household income: R9 030 + R1 100 + R1 070 = R11 200,00 per month. The gross figure may not be used because that money never reaches the household — the employer removes the deductions and pays them over on the worker's behalf, so only the net amount can actually be spent. A second error follows from the first: since the deductions never arrived as income, they must not be listed again as expenses, or the same money is subtracted twice and the family looks poorer than it is. The R1 070 from hair work also varies from month to month, so a careful budget uses the lowest recent figure or plans for its absence.

questions.question: Distinguish fixed, variable and occasional expenses, giving examples from the household budget, and explain the test used to classify an item such as prepaid electricity.
questions.expected_answer: Fixed expenses arrive at the same amount each month regardless of behaviour: rent R3 400, the funeral policy R210, school fees R520 and the phone contract R229, totalling R4 359,00. Variable expenses change with how much is used or bought: groceries R2 750, prepaid electricity R820, taxi fare R940, airtime and data R260, and toiletries and cleaning R330, totalling R5 100,00. Occasional expenses arrive only a few times a year but are provided for monthly — R350 for uniforms and stationery and R450 for December, totalling R800,00 — and setting money aside in advance like this is called provisioning. The classification test is not "does it come every month?" but "does the amount change with how much I use?" Electricity is bought monthly yet the amount responds to use, so it is variable; rent arrives monthly and responds to nothing the family does, so it is fixed. The distinction matters because when money runs short, only the variable items can be cut within the month.

questions.question: A koeksister stall has fixed costs of R720,00 a month, a variable cost of R2,80 per koeksister and a selling price of R6,50. Calculate the break-even point, explain how and why you round it, and find the profit in a month when 360 koeksisters are sold.
questions.expected_answer: Each koeksister contributes R6,50 − R2,80 = R3,70 towards the fixed costs, so the break-even number is R720 ÷ R3,70 = 194,59. This must be rounded UP to 195. At 194 the income is 194 × R6,50 = R1 261,00 against a total cost of R720 + (194 × R2,80) = R720 + R543,20 = R1 263,20 — still a loss of R2,20 — while at 195 the income is R1 267,50 against a total cost of R720 + R546,00 = R1 266,00, a profit of R1,50. For 360 koeksisters: income = 360 × R6,50 = R2 340,00; total cost = R720 + (360 × R2,80) = R720 + R1 008,00 = R1 728,00; profit = R2 340 − R1 728 = R612,00. The answer should close with a sentence: the stall breaks even at 195 koeksisters a month and, selling about 360, makes a profit of R612,00.
